shortIntro: A good match for those who enjoy big-city life and an active urban lifestyle.
longIntro: Gyeonggi-do, together with Seoul and Incheon, is also known as the Seoul Metropolitan or Capital Area.
The concentration of prestigious universities and convenient infrastructure has made it the most populated area in Korea, with 51% of the country's population (26.3M out of 51.8M) living here.
With Seoul being the country's most well-known and crowded city, many satellite cities are being built and the subway network continues to expand to ease population concentration.

shortIntro: A good match for those who enjoy both summer and winter outdoor activities.
longIntro: Gangwon-do is the Korean region with both the highest density of mountains and plenty of beaches. That makes it especially suitable for those who prefer outdoor activities — hiking, surfing and winter sports — over big city vibes. Gangneung is also known for its strong coffee culture and sea-view cafes.

Reachable within a few hours from the capital region, it's a popular leisure destination for Koreans, so expect it to get more crowded on weekends and public holidays. Developed coworking spaces are rare, but every city has plenty of study cafés that offer quite similar facilities.

shortIntro: A good match for those who prefer focused work and occasional nature escapes.
longIntro: Chungcheong-do is Korea's central region with an active international airport. The region is known for its relaxed pace of life, which is even reflected in the local dialect.

Northern Chungcheong (Chungcheongbuk-do) is the only region in Korea without access to the sea. Instead, it is famous for canyons, lakes, and scenic mountain passes, including Dodamsambong Peaks, Chungjuho, and Maltijae Observatory.

Southern Chungcheong (Chungcheongnam-do) is home to research and administrative cities, as well as historic, culinary and coastal sites. Gongju, a former Baekje Kingdom capital (475–538 CE), hosts UNESCO World Heritage sites such as Gongsanseong Fortress and the Tomb of King Muryeong. Further west, the Taean coastline area has Mongsanpo Mudflat, a popular spot for beginner-friendly clam digging, while Daecheon Beach in Boryeong has an annual Mud Festival and a ziptrek over the sea.

shortIntro: A good match for history lovers and those who enjoy big coastal cities.
longIntro: Gyeongsang-do is Korea's second major region, with a high concentration of modern big cities and important historic sites. Koreans often describe people from this region as strong and direct, but also passionate and warm-hearted.

Northern Gyeongsang (Gyeongsangbuk-do) is rich in historic sites. Gyeongju is known for preserving a thousand years of Silla history (57 BCE–935 CE). Andong is home to Hahoe Village (14th–15th centuries), a UNESCO World Heritage ↗ hanok village in a river bend where residents still live. The city also hosts an annual autumn Maskdance Festival ↗.
Southern Gyeongsang (Gyeongsangnam-do), together with Busan and Ulsan, forms a highly urbanized coastal belt with a mix of city life and natural landscapes.

shortIntro: A good match for lovers of food, history, hiking and a somewhat slower pace of life.
longIntro: Jeolla-do is often considered Korea's gourmet food region.

Northern Jeolla (Jeollabuk-do) is closely associated with the origins of the Joseon dynasty, which ruled Korea for almost five hundred years. It is also home to the largest urban hanok (traditional Korean house) village.

Southern Jeolla (Jeollanam-do) combines Gwangju, a major center of democracy and the arts, with a more natural landscape: Jirisan, the highest peak on the Korean mainland, Boseong's green tea plantations, national parks and night sea views.
Keep in mind that getting around the region can be less convenient than getting to Seoul or Busan.

shortIntro: A good match for nature lovers and a popular Korean workation destination.
longIntro: Jeju-do is a volcanic island and a popular travel and workation destination for Koreans. Some Korean companies even offer one-month work-from-Jeju programs as an employee benefit.

The island is best known for Hallasan, the country's highest point, its island-loop coastal Olle trail, flower blossoms all year round, surfing beaches and scenic ocean roads. Jeju-do also produces most of Korea's tangerines and is home to haenyeo, women freedivers known for harvesting seafood that you can enjoy fresh.

There are only two major cities, but you can also stay in smaller coastal villages, many of which are full of sea-view cafés. While a car is the easiest way to explore the island, the bus network is also well developed.
Keep in mind that the weather can sometimes be harsh and windy.
